sections.normalized_html:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry.

Therefore, the leading entries of the [MATH: 1]st, [MATH: 3]rd and [MATH: 4]th rows of [MATH: A] are [MATH: -1], [MATH: -4] and [MATH: 8], respectively.

[MATH: [− 1|1|0|1; 0|0|7|8; 0|− 4|2|4; 0|0|8|4]]

So, the answer is [MATH: -1+(-4)+8=3.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider our matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] once more, with the leading entries highlighted.

Content:
[MATH: [2|6|7|8; 0|3|6|9; 0|1|4|7; 0|0|5|8]]

Content:
We say that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

Content:
1. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
2. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

Content:
Here, [MATH: B] is in row echelon form since both conditions are satisfied. However, [MATH: A] is not in row echelon form since condition II is violated: the leading entry of the third row [MATH: (a_{32}={\color{red}1})] is placed just below the leading entry of the second row [MATH: (a_{22}=3).]

Content:
Generally speaking, row echelon form means that we have stairs where each step (represented by a leading entry [MATH: \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\large\ast}]) has a height of [MATH: 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1aa4748e1fed8ae5484393f753effb8d]

Content:
Finally, an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if the coefficient matrix (i.e., the part that is to the left of the vertical bar) is in row echelon form.

Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

[MATH: 2|1; 0|0; 0|3]

Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

[MATH: 2|1; 0|0; 0|3]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.

  2. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

  • The matrix [MATH: A] is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated). [MATH: 2|1; 0|0; 0|3]

  • The matrix [MATH: B] is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied). [MATH: 0|2|7|10; 0|0|0|0]

  • The matrix [MATH: C] is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied). [MATH: 2|0|0|0|4|6; 0|0|3|3|6|0; 0|0|0|0|4|8]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

  1. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.

  2. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

  • The first matrix is not in row echelon form since [MATH: a_{32} \neq 0] (condition II is violated). [MATH: 1|2|− 1|0; 0|1|0|1; 0|1|1|1]

  • The second matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied). [MATH: 1|2|− 1|5; 0|2|0|− 2; 0|0|1|7]

  • The third matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied). [MATH: 1|0|− 1|4; 0|1|0|1; 0|0|0|0]

  • The fourth matrix is not in row echelon form since, for example, the leading entry [MATH: a_{22}] lies to the left of the leading entry [MATH: a_{13}] (condition II is violated). [MATH: 0|0|1|1; 0|1|0|1; 1|1|1|1]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the following matrices:
[MATH: [2|6|7|8; 0|3|6|9; 0|1|4|7; 0|0|5|8]]

Content:
The first non-zero entry on each row (from left to right) is called the leading entry of that row.

Content:
- In the matrix [MATH: A,] the leading entries are [MATH: a_{11}=2,] [MATH: a_{22}=3,] [MATH: a_{32}=1,] and [MATH: a_{43}=5.]
- In the matrix [MATH: B,] the leading entries are [MATH: b_{11}=1,] [MATH: b_{22}=3,] [MATH: b_{33}=-2,] and [MATH: b_{44}=2.] The [MATH: 5]th row has no leading entry.

Content:
The leading entries are highlighted below.

Content:
[MATH: [2|6|7|8; 0|3|6|9; 0|1|4|7; 0|0|5|8]]

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying the Leading Entries of a Matrix

Example Prompt:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the [MATH: 1]st, [MATH: 3]rd and [MATH: 4]th rows in the matrix [MATH: A,] given below?
[MATH: [− 1|1|0|1; 0|0|7|8; 0|− 4|2|4; 0|0|8|4]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry.

Therefore, the leading entries of the [MATH: 1]st, [MATH: 3]rd and [MATH: 4]th rows of [MATH: A] are [MATH: -1], [MATH: -4] and [MATH: 8], respectively.

[MATH: [− 1|1|0|1; 0|0|7|8; 0|− 4|2|4; 0|0|8|4]]

So, the answer is [MATH: -1+(-4)+8=3.]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Row Echelon Form

Content:
Let's consider our matrices [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] once more, with the leading entries highlighted.

Content:
[MATH: [2|6|7|8; 0|3|6|9; 0|1|4|7; 0|0|5|8]]

Content:
We say that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

Content:
1. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
2. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

Content:
Here, [MATH: B] is in row echelon form since both conditions are satisfied. However, [MATH: A] is not in row echelon form since condition II is violated: the leading entry of the third row [MATH: (a_{32}={\color{red}1})] is placed just below the leading entry of the second row [MATH: (a_{22}=3).]

Content:
Generally speaking, row echelon form means that we have stairs where each step (represented by a leading entry [MATH: \bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\large\ast}]) has a height of [MATH: 1.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1aa4748e1fed8ae5484393f753effb8d]

Content:
Finally, an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if the coefficient matrix (i.e., the part that is to the left of the vertical bar) is in row echelon form.

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Matrices in Row Echelon Form

Example Prompt:
Which of the following matrices are in row echelon form?

[MATH: 2|1; 0|0; 0|3]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

1. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
2. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix [MATH: A] is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).
[MATH: 2|1; 0|0; 0|3]
- The matrix [MATH: B] is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).
[MATH: 0|2|7|10; 0|0|0|0]
- The matrix [MATH: C] is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).
[MATH: 2|0|0|0|4|6; 0|0|3|3|6|0; 0|0|0|0|4|8]

Item 9 — Example: Identifying Augmented Matrices in Row Echelon Form

Example Prompt:
Which of the following augmented matrices are in row echelon form?
[MATH: 1|2|− 1|0; 0|1|0|1; 0|1|1|1]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

1. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
2. Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The first matrix is not in row echelon form since [MATH: a_{32} \neq 0] (condition II is violated).
[MATH: 1|2|− 1|0; 0|1|0|1; 0|1|1|1]
- The second matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).
[MATH: 1|2|− 1|5; 0|2|0|− 2; 0|0|1|7]
- The third matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).
[MATH: 1|0|− 1|4; 0|1|0|1; 0|0|0|0]
- The fourth matrix is not in row echelon form since, for example, the leading entry [MATH: a_{22}] lies to the left of the leading entry [MATH: a_{13}] (condition II is violated).
[MATH: 0|0|1|1; 0|1|0|1; 1|1|1|1]
